predecessors.note: France gave Spain 'the country known as Louisiana, as well as New Orleans and the island in which the city is situated' (Fontainebleau, signed 3 November 1762). The Treaty of Paris (February 1763) 'divided Louisiana at the Mississippi': the east bank went to Britain and is not Spanish Louisiana. Cliopatria's New France row (1609-1791) is the French colony this land comes from.

keyframe_review.note: Spanish Louisiana: the page's infobox area is 878,745 sq mi (2,275,940 km2); the gazetteer's Louisiana region is about 2.60 M km2 (ratio 1.14, inside the factor of two), so the region slightly over-reaches. The page says the 'treaties never defined the boundaries precisely'; Lower Louisiana was roughly the part south of 31 N (a French definition), and in 1772 Unzaga set the line between Upper and Lower Louisiana at 36 35 N. The east bank went to Britain in 1763; New Orleans and its island stayed Spanish. fx-32 (F185): the northern edge is cut at the Hudson Bay drainage divide, rupert-s-land's southern border (the Rupert's Land page, opened 2026-11-01: 'The southern border, west of Lake of the Woods to the Rocky Mountains was the drainage divide' until the Convention of 1818 substituted the 49th parallel; this page says the province stretched 'to Canada's border' and names no other northern line). The whole-state North Dakota and Minnesota of the gazetteer's Louisiana region had put the Red River basin in both dossiers (1,019 cells). The Minnesota east of the Mississippi (British from 1763) is still in the region and is not part of this fix.

ledger.note: 1762 (3 November): France secretly cedes Louisiana to Spain. The treaty 'signed on November 3, 1762' gave Spain 'the country known as Louisiana, as well as New Orleans and the island in which the city is situated'; Charles ratified on 13 November, Louis ten days later (the Louisiana page's infobox: 'Transfer by France: 23 November 1762'). Spain took possession only later ('Antonio de Ulloa assumed his role as Louisiana's first Spanish governor in 1766'; O'Reilly in 1769).

ledger.note: 1768: the colonists of New Orleans rise against Spain. 'Colonists in western Louisiana rebelled in 1768 and expelled the first Spanish governor.' The page names no territory beyond the colony; New Orleans is the zone as the Louisiana page has the uprising there.

ledger.note: 1769: O'Reilly crushes the uprising. 'The 1768 uprising was not suppressed until 1769, when Alejandro O'Reilly, the second governor, successfully suppressed the uprising'; he 'took formal possession for Spain in 1769' (Fontainebleau page); Unzaga then installed Spanish law.

ledger.note: 1801 (21 March): Spanish Louisiana is returned to France. 'Retroceded back to France under the terms of the Third Treaty of San Ildefonso' (1800); the infobox gives 'Returned to France: 21 March 1801' (Treaty of Aranjuez). The page's text dates the secret transfer to 1800. Spanish officials stayed on until the handovers of 30 November 1803 (New Orleans cabildo) and 9-10 March 1804 (St. Louis, Three Flags Day).

wars.name: Louisiana Rebellion of 1768
wars.outcome: The colonists expelled Governor Ulloa in 1768; O'Reilly suppressed the uprising and took possession in 1769.

wars.name: Spanish campaigns against British West Florida
wars.outcome: Bernardo de Gálvez declared war on Britain on 8 May 1779 and won at Baton Rouge, Mobile and Pensacola, 'reclaiming Florida for Spain in 1781', recognised by the 1783 Treaty of Paris.
wars.note: Fought from Louisiana; the land won is treated in the Spanish Florida dossier, not as Spanish Louisiana.

certainty.note: The page says the treaties 'never defined the boundaries precisely'; only the Mississippi line with British (later US) land, set in 1763, is firm.

notes:
Written by am-06-x from two pages (budget 2-5). Not settled:
(1) The shape is the gazetteer's Louisiana region (west of the Mississippi) plus New Orleans' island; no page gives a boundary, and Spain held little of it beyond the river towns, the Illinois villages and Natchitoches. The 1772 line between Upper and Lower Louisiana (36 35 N) is internal.
(2) The end: the infobox gives 21 March 1801 (Treaty of Aranjuez) and the text 1800; Spanish administration lasted to 30 November 1803 and 9-10 March 1804. The dossier ends in 1801 to match the infobox; the french-louisiana dossier (am-06-c, Cliopatria 1800-1804) draws the Spanish administration as an occupation. If the reviewers prefer a Spanish colour to the actual handovers, extend this dossier's end to 1803-11 / 1804-03.
(3) Spanish West Florida (Baton Rouge, Mobile, Pensacola, 1779-1781) and the 1795 Treaty of San Lorenzo border are left to a Spanish Florida dossier; the Louisiana page is silent on whether West Florida was part of the Louisiana government. Counterpart 'Louisiana colonists (1768 rebellion)' is a name, not a dossier.
(4) The Louisiana page says Louisiana was 'a province of New Spain from 1762 to 1801'; the New Spain dossier leaves it out to avoid double drawing. The Louisiana page's remark that the Adams-Onis Treaty and 'the 1819 agreement set later limits at the Red River and Sabine' concerns Texas, not Louisiana; the Texas side is in the New Spain dossier.
